analogy.p: A cell is like a waterfall between two pools: the bigger the height difference (the gap in reactivity between the metals) the more energy each litre of water (each coulomb of charge) delivers. Stacking cells in series is like stacking waterfalls on top of each other so the total drop adds. A non-rechargeable cell is a one-way waterfall that stops when the upper pool is empty (a reactant used up); a rechargeable cell is one where a pump (the external current) lifts the water back to the top. The analogy breaks down because in a real cell electrons move in the wire but ions, not water, carry charge inside the electrolyte.

bullets: A **cell** converts **chemical energy** from reactions into **electrical energy**.
A **simple cell** = two different metals (electrodes) + an electrolyte + connecting wires.
**Voltage** of a cell depends on the **type of electrode** (which metals) and the **electrolyte**.
A **battery** = two or more cells in **series**, so the voltages **add**.
**Non-rechargeable (e.g. alkaline):** reactions stop when a reactant is used up.
**Rechargeable:** an external electrical current **reverses** the chemical reactions, so the cell can be used again.
Linked topic: hydrogen **fuel cells** (own spec point) are an alternative to rechargeable cells and batteries.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: AQA expects you to explain how **cells and batteries** produce electricity from chemical reactions. A **cell** contains chemicals that react to produce electricity. A **simple cell** is made by connecting **two different metals** in contact with an **electrolyte**, and its **voltage depends on factors including the type of electrode and the type of electrolyte**. A **battery** is **two or more cells connected together in series** to give a greater voltage. You must also distinguish **non-rechargeable** from **rechargeable** cells and batteries and explain why each behaves as it does.

bullets: Example: **magnesium** (more reactive) and **copper** (less reactive) in salt solution: Mg → Mg2+ + 2e-.
**Electrons** flow through the **wire** from the **more reactive metal** to the **less reactive metal**.
**Ions** (not electrons) move through the **electrolyte**, completing the circuit.
The reaction happens only while the circuit is **complete**; with the switch open there is no current.
The more reactive metal is **used up** (it dissolves/corrodes), which is why cells eventually go flat.
Energy transfer: **chemical energy store → electrical energy** (then to the thermal/light/kinetic energy of the device).
Write 'electrons flow in the wire' and 'ions move in the electrolyte': never mix them up.
core.h: How a simple cell works: chemical energy to electrical energy
core.p: In a simple cell two metals of **different reactivity** dip into an electrolyte. The more reactive metal tends to lose electrons more readily: its atoms form positive ions that go into the solution (the metal is **oxidised**). The electrons it leaves behind build up on that electrode, making it the **negative terminal**. If the two electrodes are joined by a wire, these electrons flow through the wire to the less reactive metal, the positive terminal. That flow of electrons through the external circuit is the **electric current**, and the potential difference that pushes it is the **voltage** of the cell.

bullets: Same metal at both electrodes → **0 V**.
Different metals, **large reactivity gap** (e.g. Mg and Cu) → **bigger voltage**; small gap (e.g. Fe and Sn) → smaller voltage.
Suitable electrolytes: **salt solution, dilute acid, copper(II) sulfate solution**, or a paste containing ions.
**Unsuitable electrolytes:** pure/distilled water (very few ions) and sugar or ethanol solutions (no ions).
The electrolyte must not be a **solid ionic compound**, because its ions cannot move.
Swapping which metal is connected to which terminal of the voltmeter **reverses the sign** of the reading, showing which metal is more reactive.
core.h: Why two different metals and an electrolyte are needed
core.p: If both electrodes are the **same metal** each has the same tendency to lose electrons, so there is **no potential difference** and no current. The **greater the difference in reactivity** between the two metals, the greater the push on the electrons, and the **higher the voltage**. The **electrolyte** is an ionic solution (or paste) that contains **free-moving ions**; these carry charge between the electrodes inside the cell, and also take part in the electrode reactions. Without free ions, the circuit cannot be completed.

bullets: **Type of electrode:** a pair of metals that are **far apart in the reactivity series** gives a higher voltage.
**Type of electrolyte:** different ions give different electrode reactions and a different voltage.
**Concentration of electrolyte:** more ions can mean a better current and a slightly different reading.
**Surface area and distance between electrodes** affect how much **current** flows (and the voltage when current is drawn).
**Temperature** can have a small effect on the reaction rate.
To **compare** metals fairly you must keep everything else (electrolyte, concentration, volume, depth of electrodes) the same.
core.h: Factors that affect the voltage of a simple cell
core.p: The specification states the voltage depends on a number of factors **including the type of electrode and the type of electrolyte**. The electrode metals decide how strongly electrons are pushed round the circuit, and the electrolyte affects how easily ions move and what reactions can happen at the electrodes. In practice other factors, such as concentration and the size of the electrodes, also change the **current** that can be drawn and can alter the measured voltage slightly.

bullets: Series: total voltage = **sum** of the cells' voltages. 4 x 1.5 V = **6.0 V**.
A **single** AA 'battery' is technically a **cell** (1.5 V).
Higher voltage lets a battery push a larger current through the same resistance (V = I R).
**Car battery:** six lead-acid cells x 2 V = 12 V.
A **9 V battery** has six 1.5 V cells in series.
Cells must be connected the **right way round** (+ to -), otherwise the voltages partly cancel.
Connecting cells in series does **not** make the cells last longer, only gives more voltage.
core.p: A **battery** is two or more cells connected together, normally in **series** (the positive terminal of one joined to the negative terminal of the next). In series the **voltages add**, so a battery gives a **greater voltage** than one cell. This is why a 9 V battery contains six 1.5 V cells and why a 12 V car battery contains six 2 V lead-acid cells. The word 'battery' is often used loosely for a single cell, but in science it means more than one cell.

bullets: The reactions stop **when a reactant is used up**, not because 'energy runs out' in general.
**Alkaline batteries** are non-rechargeable; they are cheap, store well and are useful in low-use items such as remote controls.
Trying to recharge them is unsafe and does not work properly.
They have to be **replaced**, creating waste; many contain metals that must be disposed of or recycled properly.
The voltage stays fairly steady until the reactant runs out, and then falls.
Advantage: usually **cheaper to buy** and good for devices that are rarely used.
core.p: In **non-rechargeable** (single-use) cells and batteries the chemical reactions that produce electricity are **one-way**. They carry on until **one of the reactants has been used up**, at which point the cell can no longer produce a potential difference and is described as 'flat'. **Alkaline batteries** are the standard example named in the specification: they use zinc and manganese dioxide with an alkaline electrolyte. The products cannot be turned back into reactants by passing a current through them, so they must be replaced.

bullets: **Discharging:** chemical energy → electrical energy (reactants → products).
**Charging:** electrical energy from the mains → chemical energy (products → reactants).
Examples: **lithium-ion** (phones, laptops, electric cars, about 3.7 V per cell) and **lead-acid** (car batteries, 2 V per cell).
The reversal works only if the products stay in the cell and are in a form that can be converted back.
Over many cycles the electrodes degrade, so capacity falls and the battery eventually must be replaced.
Advantage: **can be reused many times**, so fewer need to be made and thrown away; disadvantage: **higher initial cost** and need a charger.
core.p: **Rechargeable** cells and batteries (such as lithium-ion and lead-acid) can be recharged because the chemical reactions are **reversed when an external electrical current is supplied**. During **discharge** (use) the reactants form products and electrical energy is produced. During **charging** an external supply forces current through the cell the opposite way, turning the products back into reactants, so electrical energy is stored again as chemical energy. They can be used many times, though they gradually lose capacity.

bullets: **Alkaline:** low cost, no charger needed; but single use, so waste and resources used repeatedly.
**Rechargeable:** reusable many times, cheaper over time; but higher cost, needs charging, limited number of cycles.
**Fuel cell (linked topic):** keeps producing electricity as long as fuel (hydrogen) is supplied; produces **water** only; but hydrogen is hard to store and make.
Environmental: making batteries uses **metals that are mined**; disposal needs care to avoid pollution.
Use evidence-based phrases: 'although ... , however ...' to show balanced evaluation.
A **conclusion** is required in 6-mark answers: say which is best **for the stated use** and why.
core.h: Evaluating cells: non-rechargeable, rechargeable and fuel cells
core.p: Evaluation questions ask you to **weigh up** advantages and disadvantages using criteria such as cost, lifespan, convenience and environmental impact. For batteries, no option is best everywhere: alkaline cells suit low-cost, occasional use, while rechargeable batteries suit devices used heavily. A **hydrogen fuel cell** is a third option: it is not recharged but is supplied continuously with hydrogen and oxygen, and its only product is water.

bullets: **Method:** clean the metal strips with sandpaper; place a reference metal (e.g. copper) and the test metal in a beaker of electrolyte; connect to a voltmeter with crocodile leads; read the voltage.
**Independent variable:** the test metal. **Dependent variable:** voltage (V).
**Control variables:** same electrolyte and concentration, same volume, same size of electrodes, same depth, same distance apart.
**Repeat** each pair and calculate a mean to improve reliability; spot anomalies.
**Safety:** wear eye protection; use dilute acid or salt solution only; avoid short-circuiting cells.
**Conclusion:** the further apart the metals in the reactivity series, the higher the voltage.
core.h: Required skills: investigating the voltage of simple cells
core.p: A typical practical uses a pair of metal strips in an electrolyte, connected to a **voltmeter**. The **independent variable** is the metal used as the second electrode (or the electrolyte), the **dependent variable** is the **voltage in volts**, and everything else is a **control variable**. This builds the skills of planning, measuring accurately, recording results in a table, and drawing conclusions about the reactivity series.

bullets: Highest voltage with copper = **most reactive** metal of those tested.
A **reading of 0 V** means the two electrodes are the same metal (or equally reactive).
If the voltmeter reads **negative**, the leads are connected the wrong way round: the metal attached to the negative terminal is actually the less reactive one.
When describing a trend: 'as the reactivity of metal X increases, the voltage increases'.
Give **units** (V) and compare using numbers: 'Mg/Cu gave 1.8 V compared with 0.7 V for Fe/Cu'.
**Anomaly:** an outlier reading that does not fit the pattern; repeat it or ignore it when calculating the mean.
core.p: Questions often give a table or bar chart of voltages for different metal pairs. The metal that is **more reactive** is the **negative terminal**, and a larger voltage means a **greater difference in reactivity**. You can use a series of results with one common metal to place unknown metals into an order of reactivity. Always quote the **numbers** with units in your answer.

bullets: Zinc electrode: **Zn → Zn2+ + 2e-** (oxidation, zinc loses electrons).
Copper electrode in copper(II) sulfate: **Cu2+ + 2e- → Cu** (reduction, copper ions gain electrons).
In dilute acid at the less reactive metal: **2H+ + 2e- → H2** (hydrogen gas forms).
Remember **OIL RIG:** Oxidation Is Loss (of electrons); Reduction Is Gain.
The overall reaction is the same as a **displacement reaction**, but the electrons are made to travel through a wire.
This is why the order of voltages follows the **reactivity series**.
core.h: Extension: half equations at the electrodes (to explain the chemistry)
core.p: The electrode reactions in a simple cell are **oxidation and reduction** reactions (redox). At the more reactive metal, atoms **lose electrons** (oxidation). At the other electrode, something gains those electrons (reduction). Writing the half equations helps you explain **why** electrons flow. This goes slightly beyond the minimum wording of the specification for cells, but it uses ideas you meet in electrolysis and reactivity.

bullets: **Electrolysis vs cells:** electrolysis uses **electrical energy to cause** a reaction; a cell uses a **reaction to produce** electrical energy.
**Physics link:** potential difference (V), current (I), series circuits and energy transfers.
**Reactivity series:** used to predict which metal is the negative terminal.
**Fuel cells:** continuous reactant supply instead of recharging.
Typical question styles: 'State what a cell contains' (1), 'Explain why the voltage is higher for X' (2-3), 'Evaluate rechargeable and non-rechargeable batteries' (6).
Mark scheme language: 'chemical reactions stop when a reactant is used up' (non-rechargeable); 'reactions are reversed when an external current is supplied' (rechargeable).
core.p: Cells and batteries connect chemistry with physics. The chemical reactions store energy in the **chemical energy store** and release it as **electrical energy**, which a circuit then transfers to other stores. They also link to **reactivity, displacement reactions, redox, electrolysis** (which is the reverse process using electricity to cause chemical change) and to **sustainability** through resource use and disposal. Expect short recall marks and an extended evaluation.

exam: **1 mark:** 'A cell contains chemicals that react to produce electricity' or 'a battery is two or more cells connected in series'.
**2 marks (non-rechargeable):** 'The chemical reactions stop' + 'when one of the reactants is used up'.
**2 marks (rechargeable):** 'An external electrical current is supplied' + 'which reverses the chemical reactions'.

**Voltage question (2-3 marks):** state that voltage depends on the **type of electrode** (the difference in reactivity of the two metals) and the **type of electrolyte**; use the reactivity series to justify.
**Calculation:** series battery voltage = number of cells x voltage per cell; show the working and the unit V.
**Data questions:** quote values with units, state the trend, and say which metal is more reactive.
**Practical questions:** name the independent variable (metal), dependent (voltage) and control variables (electrolyte, concentration, size and depth of electrodes).
**6-mark evaluation:** compare at least three criteria (cost, lifetime, environmental impact, convenience) for both types, then reach a justified conclusion for a named use.
**Command words:** 'State' - brief fact; 'Explain' - give reason using 'because'; 'Evaluate' - weigh pros and cons and conclude.
**Common trap:** say 'electrons' for the wire and 'ions' for the electrolyte; examiners penalise mixing them.

mistakes.r: Electrons flow through the wire; ions move through the electrolyte.
mistakes.w: Electricity flows through the electrolyte as electrons.

mistakes.r: A battery is two or more cells connected together (in series).
mistakes.w: A battery is a single cell.

mistakes.r: Two different metals are needed; the same metal gives no potential difference.
mistakes.w: Two pieces of the same metal make a cell.

mistakes.r: The chemical reactions stop when one of the reactants has been used up.
mistakes.w: Non-rechargeable batteries run out of energy.

mistakes.r: The external current reverses the chemical reactions; electrical energy is stored as chemical energy.
mistakes.w: Rechargeable batteries make or create energy when charged.

mistakes.r: The electrolyte must contain free ions (e.g. salt solution or dilute acid).
mistakes.w: Any liquid, such as sugar solution or pure water, can be the electrolyte.

mistakes.r: Series connection increases the voltage; it does not by itself increase lifetime.
mistakes.w: Adding more cells in series gives longer battery life.

mistakes.r: The more reactive metal loses electrons and is the negative terminal.
mistakes.w: The less reactive metal is the negative terminal.

mistakes.r: Fuel cells are not recharged; they are continuously supplied with fuel and oxygen.

summary: Know that a cell uses chemical reactions to produce electricity, that a simple cell is two different metals in an electrolyte whose voltage depends on the electrodes and electrolyte, and that a battery is two or more cells in series. Be able to explain why non-rechargeable cells stop when a reactant is used up while rechargeable ones can have their reactions reversed by an external current.

terms.d: A device containing chemicals that react to produce electricity.
Two or more cells connected together in series to provide a greater voltage.
Two different metals in contact with an electrolyte, connected by wires.
An ionic solution or paste containing free-moving ions that carry charge in a cell.
A conductor (here a metal) in contact with the electrolyte at which reactions occur.
The energy transferred per unit charge; the 'push' that drives current, measured in volts (V).
A cell in which the chemical reactions stop when one of the reactants has been used up.
A cell whose chemical reactions are reversed when an external electrical current is supplied.
Cells joined end to end so that their voltages add.
A list of metals in order of how readily they lose electrons to form positive ions.
A cell supplied by an external source of fuel (e.g. hydrogen) and oxygen that produces a potential difference as the fuel is oxidised.
A charged particle formed when an atom or group of atoms loses or gains electrons.

worked.ans: Magnesium and copper are further apart in the reactivity series than iron and copper, so there is a bigger difference in tendency to lose electrons and therefore a higher voltage.
worked.q: A simple cell is made from magnesium and copper in salt solution. A second cell uses iron and copper in the same solution. The first cell gives a higher voltage. Explain why. (3 marks)
steps: Voltage depends on the type of electrode.
Magnesium is much more reactive than iron, so the reactivity gap to copper is larger.
A larger difference in reactivity gives a larger potential difference.

worked.q: A battery is made by connecting 6 cells of 1.5 V in series. (a) Calculate the voltage. (b) How many 1.5 V cells in series are needed for 12 V? (3 marks)

worked.ans: Most reactive Q, then R, then P (least reactive), because the bigger the voltage with copper, the greater the difference in reactivity.
worked.q: A student connects each of three metals P, Q and R to copper in the same electrolyte and measures P/Cu = 0.4 V, Q/Cu = 1.2 V, R/Cu = 0.8 V. Put P, Q and R in order of reactivity, and explain. (3 marks)
steps: Larger voltage with copper means a larger difference in reactivity from copper.
Q gave the highest voltage (1.2 V), R next (0.8 V), P lowest (0.4 V).
Assuming all are more reactive than copper, the order is Q > R > P.
